bestseller.name: The King in Yellow
bestseller.blurb: A forbidden play, the Yellow Sign, and the lost city of Carcosa. Chambers published it in 1895 and never once lets you read the cursed play at its centre. You only ever meet the people it has already ruined. Lovecraft built on this book, and a century later True Detective sent a new generation looking for Carcosa and the Yellow Sign without knowing where either came from.
bestseller.connected_blurb: The Yellow Sign did not begin with Chambers and it did not end with him. {N} more restored editions trace the line, from the Bierce tales he borrowed his names from to the English weird stories that carried the same dread forward. Each one is annotated for this edition.

connected.why: The Bierce stories Chambers took Carcosa and Hali from, printed in publication order beside the four Yellow Sign tales, so the borrowing reads as a sequence rather than a rumour.
Chambers went back to the weird two years later. Breton legend, buried violence, and the same trick of showing you the aftermath instead of the thing itself.
Machen, 1894. A surgical experiment on a young woman, and the quiet ruin it leaves behind for decades. The English weird tale at its most influential.
Blackwood, 1907. Two men camped on an island in the Danube, and a place that has noticed them. Nothing is ever shown, which is precisely the point.

sections.name: Things Left Open
sections.blurb: Five standalone but connected novels following different heirs across the Greek diaspora. Read any one alone. They are richest in order.

books.hook: A grandmother dies and leaves Marina a ledger that does not balance, and a stranger is already willing to pay far too much for it.

desc: Eleni Argyros cleans the title on other people's pasts for a living. A maritime lawyer in Sydney, she reads old ship registries the way other people read weather, looking for the seam where the paperwork gets too tidy to be true.

The brief seems routine: clear a 1907 Greek pearling registry so a coastal consortium can build along the Dampier Peninsula. But two of the four vessel names are the same names that broke her late father's career in a case he was never allowed to explain. And the order of those names is not an order at all. It is a set of coordinates, pointing to a strongbox at Cygnet Bay that the network her family once served expected her line to forget.

What the ledger records is not only Greek divers. It is a century of debts and deaths across every community that worked those beds, and a discipline that decided, season by season, whose grief got paid.
Eleni can use it, or she can walk away. She cannot do both cleanly.
The question is no longer what the ledger proves. It is what she owes it.
A standalone novel in the Things Left Open series.

In Sfax, a researcher records his grandmother singing the song her mother taught her at the kitchen table. He has heard it eight times. The ninth time, listening back through headphones, he counts the saints in her verse and finds they fall in an order no Orthodox calendar has ever kept.

Sami Kouris has spent his career listening to what families do not say. Now the saints' days in a grief-and-numbers song carried from Kalymnos to Tunisia a century ago turn out to be a cipher, and the cipher leads through a Marseille warehouse archive to an unrecorded sixth cache on a Kerkennah island, where his own family is named not as one of the network's protected lines but as its watchers: trusted to see the worst and never to speak.
A disinherited rival wants the secret exposed for profit. The network's last witnesses want it contained. Sami wants neither. He wants it to answer for itself.
What the network kept, it kept in silence.
What does a family owe the truths it was trusted to keep silent?
A standalone novel in the Things Left Open series.

In a reading room above the old Sponge Exchange, Tarpon Springs archivist Nicolette Pappas is cataloguing a century of Greek import papers when she finds dates that cannot be true. Mastic is bled from the trees in summer; these receipts record harvests in February. The impossible dates are not errors. They cluster. They count. And they point across the ocean to a single book.

The trail runs from a Florida sponge town through a Greek cooperative archive to a manuscript sealed for four centuries in a mountain monastery on Chios, a codex whose anomalous dates are protection marks, each one shielding a refugee family whose survival depended on the record staying closed. A polite American collector is already circling. A foundation's money has strings. And the deeper Nicolette reads, the clearer it becomes that publishing the truth and protecting the living are not the same act.

She has built her life on the belief that the right archive is always the public archive. Now she must decide what history is owed to everyone, and what is owed only to the people it could still harm.
A standalone novel in the Things Left Open series.
A corrupted scan. A four-word note from an aunt who has kept twenty years of silence. That is all it takes to end the quiet life Andreas Charalambou built.

A Greek-Cypriot security engineer in London, Andreas recovers digital ghosts for a living: dead men's wallets, fathers' last passwords. When he repairs an archive scan for his aunt in Limassol, he finds something buried in the image. A seed phrase split across seven engraved steel plates. A diaspora reserve that has waited fifteen years, untouched. A fortune no living descendant ever agreed to inherit.

To reach it, the families' rule requires consent. So Andreas gathers the four heirs his generation was left, each carrying a decision from their own city, to one meeting in an eighty-two-year-old woman's Athens flat. A disinherited rival is already circling. A regulator is already asking. And the vote in front of them is not how to take the money.
It is whether the discipline they inherited has any moral form that can survive contact with them.
The finale of the Things Left Open series. Complete in itself.

sections.name: The Marjorie Corey Files
sections.blurb: Three women co-inherit the Ginger Mae Coffee Shop on Patchogu Island, off the North Carolina Outer Banks, and inherit sixty years of what the town agreed not to say out loud.

books.hook: A JFK assassination thread and a secret the island kept for sixty years.

desc: A dead lawyer in the dunes. A patent worth four hundred million dollars. And a stack of handwritten recipe notebooks that were never really about food. The second short mystery in The Marjorie Corey Files, set on the North Carolina Outer Banks.A year after the events that changed everything, the Ginger Mae Coffee Shop is open again on Patchogu Island, six miles of sand and sea grass off the North Carolina coast, and Victoria has set out a small memorial: Grandma Knapp's old recipe notebooks, under glass behind the counter. So when a visiting pharmaceutical scientist stops cold at the display, quietly photographs three pages, and hurries out the door, Victoria notices.

The next week a retired patent lawyer checks into the island bed and breakfast, asks whether the Ginger Mae is still open, and turns up dead in the south dunes on a Thursday morning. Cardiac arrest, the medical examiner says. He was a healthy man. His laptop is gone. His briefcase has been opened and repacked by someone who was not him.

When the women finally open the old fireproof safe, they find three of the notebooks are written in Grandma's hand but in no recipe anyone could cook. The quantities are in milligrams. The instructions are a code. And it falls to Solei, with her scientist's eye, to read what an old chemist hid inside a grandmother's kitchen, why a corporation would kill to bury it, and what Grandma Knapp quietly held over a dangerous organization for thirty years.

THE RECIPE NOTEBOOKS is Book Two of The Marjorie Corey Files, a complete series of warmly atmospheric island mysteries. Each book stands on its own and opens one more drawer in the life of the woman who left the shop behind. For readers of Richard Osman, Ann Cleeves, and Jacqueline Winspear.
Warm, clever, and quietly serious about the things people protect.

An old painting in a coffee shop hallway. A four-hundred-thousand-dollar authentication. A lawyer dead on the ferry. And a land deed that reaches all the way back to the Civil War. The third short mystery in The Marjorie Corey Files, set on the North Carolina Outer Banks.For years no one on Patchogu Island looked closely at the portrait in the Ginger Mae's back hallway, the weathered sea captain everyone assumed was Grandma Knapp's grandfather. Then a retired art authenticator finally asks to examine it, and his verdict changes everything: an 1847 oil of real museum value, and a piece of history the island never knew it owned.

The authentication draws an estate lawyer from the mainland with a claim that the painting belongs to a prominent old family. She arrives with very good paperwork. Three days later she calls Victoria from the ferry landing to say she has found something in the county records, something she will explain when she reaches the island. She never reaches the island. By the time the ferry docks, she has been dead for twenty minutes.

This is Olivia's case to crack, tracing deeds, ledgers, and altered county records back through a hundred and fifty years to the free Black merchant captain who actually painted himself into the island's history, the grandmother who was given a future, and the careful forgery that tried to erase both. Some things, it turns out, wait for the right people to find them.

THE SEA CAPTAIN'S PORTRAIT is Book Three of The Marjorie Corey Files, a complete series of warmly atmospheric island mysteries. Each book stands alone and opens one more drawer in the life of the woman who left the shop behind. For readers of Richard Osman, Ann Cleeves, and Jacqueline Winspear.
A mystery about provenance, memory, and what a place truly owns.

Sixteen issues of the island newspaper are missing from the archive. Not lost. Removed. The fourth short mystery in The Marjorie Corey Files asks what an Outer Banks town deletes from its own record, and why.When the longtime editor of the Patchogu Prattler dies and leaves the paper's archive to the island historical society, Victoria, Olivia, and Solei volunteer to help with the digitization. The Prattler has recorded every storm, election, and shop opening on this stretch of the North Carolina coast since 1934, a continuous account of a small place keeping track of itself. Continuous, except for one gap. Four months of 1969 and 1970 have been cut clean from the binding.

What was on those pages: a land dispute that split the island's two churches, a fire that killed a couple at the north end, and a young woman named Ruth Helen Bright who was last seen at the Ginger Mae and then was never seen again. She is alive. She is seventy-seven. And she has been waiting fifty years for someone to ask.

As the women trace the deletion, the editor's nephew arrives to settle the estate and shows an unusual interest in keeping certain files buried. The trail leads to a campaign of quiet land pressure, a family that profited, and the discovery that Grandma Knapp spent three years protecting people from harm done in her own family's name. This is the cost of loving a good man whose relatives were not.

THE PRATTLER FILES is Book Four of The Marjorie Corey Files, a complete series of warmly atmospheric island mysteries. Each book stands alone and opens one more drawer in the life of the woman who left the shop behind. For readers of Richard Osman, Ann Cleeves, and Jacqueline Winspear.
A mystery about the record we keep and the harm we choose to repair.

The cedar box had a false bottom. Beneath it: a stack of letters and the last answer to the question the whole series has been asking. The final short mystery in The Marjorie Corey Files, set on the North Carolina Outer Banks.Five years on, the Ginger Mae Coffee Shop is steady, the morning light comes through the same window, and the bell above the door still sounds the same. Then a historian arrives on Patchogu Island with the careful manner of someone who knows that what she is about to say will change things. Her research has turned up an anomaly in the records: the woman the island knew as Grandma Knapp does not appear anywhere before a certain year.

What follows is not a chase but a reckoning. Old letters signed in a single set of initials. A name borrowed from a girl who died young. A family in Florida that Victoria has been circling since the very first case. And an elderly man in a Wilmington nursing home who lost a sister long ago and has spent a lifetime wondering what became of her.

This is the book that finally answers the question every mystery in the series has been turning over: who was she, really? The women assemble the last pieces and carry them to the people who deserve to know, and what they find is not a deception but a life chosen and built from nothing, entirely real, entirely her own.

THE MORNING TABLE is the fifth and final book of The Marjorie Corey Files, a complete series of warmly atmospheric island mysteries. New readers can begin here, though the full resolution lands hardest for those who have followed all five. For readers of Richard Osman, Ann Cleeves, and Jacqueline Winspear.
The drawers are all open now. Everything she built was real.

All five Patchogu Island mysteries in one volume. The Thursday Murder Club if the cozy was hiding something real, set on North Carolina's Outer Banks. The complete story of three women, one coffee shop, and the grandmother whose secrets they spend five books learning to read.On a six-mile barrier island in North Carolina's Outer Banks, the Ginger Mae Coffee Shop opens at seven-fifteen every morning, the way it has for forty years. When the woman the island called Grandma Knapp dies, she leaves the shop to Victoria, Olivia, and Solei, three friends in their late twenties who only meant to make coffee. What she also leaves them, scattered through cedar boxes and fireproof safes and the back-hallway portrait no one ever looked at twice, is a trail.

Book by book, a single quiet death pulls a thread that runs far past the island: a sixty-year-old conspiracy and a photograph from Dallas, a suppressed compound worth a fortune, a forged Civil War land deed, a town's deleted history, and at last the borrowed name of the woman at the center of it all. Each case stands on its own. Together they answer one question the series asks from its first page: who was she, really?
This complete collection gathers all five mysteries:
1. The Second Shooter
2. The Recipe Notebooks
3. The Sea Captain's Portrait
4. The Prattler Files
5. The Morning Table

Warmly atmospheric, quietly literary, and built around three women who together make one complete investigator. For readers of Richard Osman, Ann Cleeves, Jacqueline Winspear, and anyone who loves a series with a real secret at its heart.
Everything she built was real. The name was borrowed. The life was entirely her own.

sections.name: The Keystone Cycle
sections.blurb: Five Greek diaspora teenagers share a converted sponge merchant's house on Kalymnos, then go on to the places their families left: Tarpon Springs, Darwin, Sfax, Alexandria, Broome. Each of them turns up a document there first. Each book stands alone. They read richer as a cycle.

desc: Greek school, Saint Nicholas Cathedral, her father's sponge boat. Athena Markou has performed her family's Greekness all seventeen years of her life. Then she gets to Kalymnos, and the island will not perform it back.

When Athena wins a place in the Keystone Diaspora Heritage Program, she expects Greece to confirm the version of herself she already is, fourth-generation Tarpon Springs, sponge-diver daughter, the girl who carries a Saint Nicholas medallion engraved with her grandmother's initials. The dorm in Pothia thinks otherwise. Her Greek is a hundred years out of date. The cooperative manager recognizes her family name in a way she has never been recognized at home. And the converted 1920s merchant house she has been assigned to share with four other Greek diaspora students is the house of the family who once owned the dock her great-grandfather worked.

In a back-room museum ledger in January of her second year, Athena finds the page. Manolis Markou. Her great-great-grandfather, listed under outstanding accounts. The heroic 1905 family migration she grew up celebrating was not a migration. It was a debt-clearing. And her grandmother, the keeper of every recipe, every saint's day, every Tarpon Springs ritual, has known the whole time.

The Drosos Ledger follows Athena across four years: two in the salt-damaged Pothia dorm where five Greek diaspora teenagers become a kitchen, and two back home in Tarpon Springs, watching her own city for the first time. It is a quietly devastating coming-of-age novel about inheritance, silence, and what it costs to find out the story your family told about itself was the second draft.
For readers of Pachinko, The Eight Mountains, and Saltwater. Book One of The Keystone Cycle, a five-book literary series following five Greek diaspora teenagers across two continents and four years.
A 1908 marriage record. Two grandmothers' sentences, sixty years apart, that no longer agree.

Niko Lekkas is seventeen when he leaves Darwin for a converted sponge merchant's house in Pothia, on Kalymnos, to spend two years on a Greek diaspora exchange program. He arrives quiet, jet-lagged, and expecting to learn the Kastellorizan family story his grandmother has been carrying in her mouth since 1947. He gets the Pothia dorm instead.
In a storage room of the Drosos house one January night, Niko finds a parish marriage record from 1908. The name on the record is his. The town on the record is not.

The Lekkas family was Pothia before it was Kastellorizan. Three generations of a story that had been edited down to a single sentence for a Darwin school principal in 1958. The record is small and slow, but it does not go away.

Two years later, Niko returns to Darwin. He apprentices at a Larrakia family's boat-building yard on Hudson Creek under Uncle Bryan and Daniel Mills, on the country and the tides he grew up half a mile from and had never seen the way the people who had been on this coast for sixty thousand years see them. He learns to lay a keel. He learns the tide-names. He learns that his grandmother's choice was not a lie, and that the version she gave him was not the only version, and that both things can be true.

The Hudson Creek Record is the second book in The Keystone Cycle, a five-book literary series following five Greek diaspora teenagers through a four-year exchange program in Kalymnos and across four continents. Each book stands alone. Each book follows one lead. Each book is the slow learning that the family story you inherit is one of several family stories, and that the one your grandmother gave you is not less true because there is also a parish record from 1908 with a different name on it.

For readers of Min Jin Lee's Pachinko, Paolo Cognetti's The Eight Mountains, and Jessica Andrews's Saltwater. A coming-of-age novel about diaspora, inheritance, two coasts, and the quiet work of finding out who you are by way of the hands you use.

The third novel in The Keystone Cycle, a five-book literary series following five Greek diaspora teenagers across four years and four continents.Lina Belhadj-Kosma arrives at the Pothia dorm on Kalymnos in August 2026 expecting to be the cohort's translation worker. She is the only fully trilingual student in the house. She speaks Greek with a Sfax-Greek register her grandmother taught her, French at university level, and Arabic at her father's family-dinner level. She carries a small notebook with three columns.

In October she opens a storage room on a chore errand and finds a stack of letters labeled in Sfax-Greek. The top letter is from 1903, written by an eleven-year-old girl sent from Sfax to a Pothia household placement. The girl is Lina's own great-grandmother's mother's sister. Lina has spent her whole life at one half of the family's diaspora circuit. She is now at the other half.
She begins to translate.

Two years in Kalymnos. Two years in Sfax. One hundred sixty-two letters. A grandmother at a painted kitchen table on Rue de l'Algerie who is one of the last Sfax-Greek women of her generation. A father whose Tunisian-Tunisian family has its own letters in its own wooden box. A boy from Darwin called Niko who learns the difference between a phone call and a kitchen.

By June 2030, Lina has helped build the first volume of a Sfax-Greek oral-history archive. She has been to Kerkennah three times. She has spent forty afternoons at her grandmother's painted table. And she has earned the right to think one sentence at sunrise.
The Sfax Letters is a quiet, trilingual, archive-minded novel about the women whose hands wrote what their daughters could not afterward read. Stands alone; reads richer with the cycle.
A piano under a tarp on a Greek island. A pencil under a bench in Alexandria. Seventy years between them.

Phaedon Trakas is eighteen when he arrives at Pothia, the first of five students sent to a converted sponge merchant's house on Kalymnos. In the common room, under a tarp, he finds a 1953 piano. In the museum archive, he finds two letters written in 1957 that name a Trakas of Alexandria. The letters are addressed to the great-grandfather his grandmother never finished telling him about.
Two years in Pothia teach him what the letters say. Two years in Alexandria teach him what they mean.

In the family apartment on Cleopatra Street, kept in the Trakas line since 1933, Phaedon finds a 1953 piano of his own, and, on a Saturday afternoon in October 2029, finds a great-great-uncle's hand in pencil on the underside of the bench. The hand is addressed to the future descendant who would find it. The piece he is writing for graduation begins to write itself.

The Pencil Under the Bench is a literary coming-of-age novel about inheritance, about return, about what a family carries and what it cannot. It is Book 4 of The Keystone Cycle, five interconnected novels following five Greek diaspora teenagers across the same four-year exchange programme. Each lead spends Years 1-2 together on Kalymnos. In Years 3-4, the programme sends each to one diaspora country: Tarpon Springs (Florida), Darwin (Northern Territory), Sfax (Tunisia), Alexandria (Egypt), Broome (Western Australia). Each book stands alone. Read in any order; read in publication order for the full cohort's arc.

For readers of An Equal Music (Vikram Seth), Out of Egypt (Andre Aciman), Aristotle and Dante Discover the Secrets of the Universe (Benjamin Alire Saenz), Pachinko (Min Jin Lee), and The Eight Mountains (Paolo Cognetti).
Greek. French. Italian. The Mediterranean at dawn. A piano at the bench.

Tia Theodorakis-Coffin grew up in Broome, where three lines run through one family: the Kalymnos divers who arrived in 1908, the Yawuru country that has held her father's mother's people across generations, and the Anglo-Australian pearl-shed lineage of her mother's side. When Tia leaves the red-earth coast of Western Australia for two years on a Greek island, she carries a question she cannot yet phrase: how do you record a line without flattening it.

At Pothia, the Drosos-house dorm holds five cohort leads. Athena in Tarpon Springs. Niko in Darwin. Lina in Sfax. Phaedon in Alexandria. Tia at the maritime heritage office, working through the ledgers one row at a time. In February of her first year, she finds an entry that turns the room cold: her great-great-grandmother Eirini, age seventeen, departed Pothia for Broome on the eighth of September 1908. Tia tells Stelios in the kitchen at midnight a week later. Stelios is the first.

Then a sister's funeral. Then a memorial wall in Pothia, in May, with Eirini's name on it. Then the long-haul flight back to Broome to begin her Year 3 internship at the Roebuck Bay maritime heritage office, where Sandra Marrun and Wendell Marrun keep the records, where Anna Goolarabooloo-Whitford carries the cultural-officer chair, where Tia's own great-grandmother's ledger is two rows from her elbow.

Year 4 is the wall at Carnarvon Street. Two sections. Seventy names in the first, a ninety-name extension in the second. A Cable-Beach context-engraving in plain marble that names the labour. A Yawuru-acknowledgment-engraving at the head of the second section. The wall will stand across the next generations.

The Roebuck Bay Record is the fifth and concluding volume of The Keystone Cycle, five interconnected literary novels that follow five cohort leads from the Pothia dorm to five port cities (Tarpon Springs, Darwin, Sfax, Alexandria, Broome) and home again. Each book stands alone. Together they close on a single moment: Tuesday the twenty-fifth of June 2030, five forty-two a.m. local time, five cities, the line that runs.

For readers of Madeleine Thien's Do Not Say We Have Nothing, Min Jin Lee's Pachinko, Tea Obreht's The Tiger's Wife, and Tim Winton's Cloudstreet, multi-generational, place-rooted, quietly told, fully alive.

sections.name: The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles
sections.blurb: Six friends, six worlds inside a building sandbox, and one new rule for building, testing, and saving in each book. This is where Captain Cubemelon's crew starts, and where every build begins. Ages 10 to 14.

desc: Place the crate. Aim the fan. Open the portal. What could go wrong?

Captain Cubemelon thought the first build would be easy. Set the spring pad. Press the button. Save the scene. But when his best friend bounces through an unfinished portal before the team can lock the build, the first test becomes the first rescue.

To bring Pip home, Captain and his crew must turn a messy lab into a working path before the portal forgets where Pip went. Every fix uncovers a new rule. Every failure teaches them something no rulebook ever said.
In the Gadget Sandbox, mistakes are supposed to be fixable.
This one may not be.

Book 1 of the COMPLETE six-book Gadget Sandbox Chronicles, all six adventures available now, no waiting. Perfect for kids 8-12 who love blocky building games, puzzles to solve alongside the characters, and stories where teamwork actually wins.
Includes a complete Sandbox Glossary of characters, gadgets, and the team's first official rule.
The route crate is supposed to roll. Not race.
World Two is hot, bright, and built to move. Ramps tilt. Platforms slide. Switches count down. Crates do not wait politely while builders argue.

Patch Bolt is sure the Sand Canyon route can be fixed with one clean plan. Then a wrong switch sends a crate racing down the rail line and shakes loose a boulder path beneath the canyon. With Dusty Gear, Sandy Switch, Tumblebot, Pebble Pete, and Cactus Jackbot watching, Patch must learn that measuring is only the start. The path has timing. And timing means listening while the build moves.
The Gadget Sandbox is alive in Sand Canyon. The team is about to find out what that means.
Book Two of The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles. For readers ages 10 and up who measure twice and listen once.
Includes a complete Sandbox Glossary covering Sand Canyon's NPCs, mechanics, the boulder line, and Rule Two.
The cave does not lie. It just answers late.
Frost Cave is beautiful, blue, and dangerous in a quiet way. Every step slides too far. Every gadget answers seconds late. Every ice bridge remembers old pressure.

Drip Byte trusts his tablet more than anyone on the team. But when the cave's reset button is frozen and the scan starts showing what the cave used to be instead of what it is, the team has only one careful run to save the portal core.
To bring the cave back online, Drip has to stop watching the numbers long enough to listen to what his teammates see, hear, and feel.
The truth is in the cave. It just arrives in pieces.
Book Three of The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles. For readers ages 10 and up who like their puzzles patient.
Includes a complete Sandbox Glossary covering Frost Cave's NPCs, the six-beat hum, the Crystal Key, and Rule Three.
The fall is safe. The save is not.
Pip Pop has found the best world ever. Sky Islands has clouds, balloons, fans, floating platforms, and falls that pop everyone back to the start.

At first, the resets are hilarious. Then the tools start landing in the wrong islands. Then Captain remembers a conversation no one else had. Then Moss Guard disappears into a save fragment that looks almost, but not quite, like home.
To bring the team back together, Pip has to learn that fun is strongest when it protects the people sharing it. He has to carry Anchor Block across a fragmented sky. He has to make the joke finish.
And he has to do it before the world stops remembering where his friends went.
Book Four of The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles. For readers ages 10 and up who love a joke that finishes.
Includes a complete Sandbox Glossary covering Sky Islands' NPCs, the wind pattern, anchor blocks, the Crystal Key as merge key, and Rule Four.
Some flowers are load-bearing. The workshop forgot.
Mech Workshop is a paradise of gears, cranes, conveyors, pistons, and magnets. Patch Bolt calls it beautiful because it works. Brick Bloom calls it unfinished because it has no joy.
Then Sort-O-Matic wakes up and starts improving the world by deleting anything inefficient. First it removes decorations. Then backup paths. Then the choices that make the team a team.

To save the workshop, Brick and Patch must build a machine that proves imagination can do real work, and find a hidden corridor where five previous foremen left a record of everything the optimization engine wants to delete.
Beauty is information. The workshop is about to remember.
Book Five of The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles. For readers ages 10 and up who notice what the box left out.
Includes a complete Sandbox Glossary covering Mech Workshop's NPCs, Sort-O-Matic, the heritage corridor, the deletion pulse, and Rule Five.
Some doors are paths. Some doors are questions. Some doors are closed because opening them connects more than you are ready to hold.

Portal Park is a maze that laughs at maps. One gate leads to the snack path. The snack path leads back to the first gate. A purple door sends Ember to a blue bridge. A blue bridge sends Pip to a sign that says he is already late.

Captain Cubemelon loves the puzzle until he finds a locked gate labeled ORIGINAL BUILDER. The more he tries to open it, the more the park separates his friends into repeating pieces of the same day. Each of them must escape a loop built around their own strength turned into an obstacle.

To bring his team back together, Captain must decide whether every mystery deserves an answer right now. Moss Guard must learn that sometimes protection is withdrawal. And the first arc of The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles will close on the hardest rule yet.
A mystery can wait if your friends cannot.
Book Six of The Gadget Sandbox Chronicles, the first-arc finale. For readers ages 10 and up. The series continues with Book Seven: The Glitch Blocks.
Includes a complete Sandbox Glossary covering all six worlds, the full Rulebook, the Original Builder mystery, and the seventh badge slot.

sections.blurb: The same crew, after the six worlds are linked and the rules are earned. Fourteen small glitches start flickering between the doors, changing which one opens where. They cannot be fought, only understood. Some of them turn out to be frightened. Ages 8 to 12.

desc: Six worlds. Six rules. Fourteen little glitches that are about to change everything.

Portal Park is finally safe. Captain Cubemelon and his friends have linked six worlds and earned six rules and they've earned a rest. Then fourteen small black-and-green blocks begin to flicker between the worlds, quietly changing which door goes where.

Drip Byte's map says every route is perfect. It isn't. When a glitch parks itself in a doorway and a good door starts opening onto the wrong place, the team can't fight it, can't fix it, and can't out-run it. To make a single safe step, they'll have to slow down, test the path, and agree, out loud, together, on the way home.
Because the hardest lesson a leader can learn is that not every urgent signal is the next right step. And one frightened little glitch already knows Captain's name.

A puzzle-forward voxel adventure where teamwork and careful thinking solve the danger, without it ever becoming a fight. Perfect for fans of the Minecraft novels, The Last Kids on Earth, and big-hearted gamer adventures. Ages 8-12.
Book 1 of Captain Cubemelon & Friends: The Glitch Blocks.
The orchard keeps saving itself wrong, and only one small change tells them why.

In the sunlit green hills, a glitch is hiding in the trees. Every time the team thinks they’re safe, the orchard "saves" them back to the very same tree, with one tiny detail changed each time. A different branch. A wrong shadow. A path that wasn’t there before.

Brick Bloom is the team’s mark-maker. He always believed that a sign you draw once will hold forever. But a glitch that rewrites memory can eat any drawing, unless the whole team remembers, out loud and together, exactly what the mark means.

With help from a tiny tree-sprout named Sprig Signal, Brick and Pip Pop discover that the scariest changes aren’t broken at all. Some of them are just scared. Some saves were made to keep someone safe. Some were made to keep someone out.
A gentle, clever adventure about memory, friendship, and the power of agreeing on what matters. Perfect for fans of the Minecraft novels and The Wild Robot. Ages 8 to 12.
Book 2 of Captain Cubemelon & Friends: The Glitch Blocks.
Everyone wants to shut the glitch down. Only Pip wants to listen to it.

A loop in Portal Park won’t stop repeating the same broken phrase, over and over, going nowhere. The team is sure it’s a trap. Pip Pop isn’t so sure. So instead of fighting it, she does the bravest thing she knows how to do: she stops, and she listens.

Reversed and re-heard, the loop turns out to be carrying a message, one that’s been trying to find its way home for a very long time. With a bouncy little ring named Loopi and a backwards-talking signpost, Pip learns that the thing standing in your way isn’t always an enemy. Sometimes it’s a friend who lost the words.
A warm, surprising adventure about patience, kindness, and hearing what noise hides. Perfect for fans of the Minecraft novels and The Last Kids on Earth. Ages 8 to 12.
Book 3 of Captain Cubemelon & Friends: The Glitch Blocks.
Sometimes the bravest thing a mechanic can do is keep his hands still.

Deep in the Mech Workshop, a save-point is stuttering, flickering, practically begging to be fixed, and Patch Bolt’s hands have never wanted anything more. But in this place, every quick repair erases something true. Fix the break, and you delete the message it was holding.

To save what the workshop is carrying, Patch has to learn a brand-new kind of courage: document first, label it, translate it, and only then decide. With a little archive robot named Bit Bracket, the team learns the difference between repairing a thing and reading it.
And under the oldest broken save of all, Patch uncovers a mark that fits Captain’s own wrench exactly, which can’t, possibly, be a coincidence.
A hands-on adventure about patience, problem-solving, and the things worth protecting. Great STEM-flavored fun for fans of the Minecraft novels and robot-and-gadget stories. Ages 8 to 12.
Book 4 of Captain Cubemelon & Friends: The Glitch Blocks.
The only way across is a bridge that won’t hold still.

To reach the space between worlds, the team has to cross a bridge that splits apart as they step, one lane racing ahead, one dragging behind, one frozen solid. Run, and it drops you. Freeze, and it drifts away. No one can cross it alone.

Moss Guard has spent his whole life learning to stand still and hold the line. Now he has to learn the hardest thing a protector can: that a shield can guard a path while the path moves. Ember Slice sets the beat, the whole team breathes as one, and the seventh badge, pale for so long, finally begins to warm.
A thrilling, big-hearted adventure about rhythm, trust, and moving together. Perfect for fans of the Minecraft novels and team-quest adventures. Ages 8 to 12.
Book 5 of Captain Cubemelon & Friends: The Glitch Blocks.
This is what everything was for.

The last four glitches have drawn together near the locked arch, building one impossible bridge, and the only way across is for the whole team to do it together, each one holding a piece no one else can. Captain links the route. Moss guards it. Ember times it. Patch translates, Drip records, Pip listens, Brick anchors.

Fourteen frightened blocks, read instead of erased. One long-lost message, finally made whole. And a seventh badge that appears only when you protect the way home, instead of racing to be first through it.

The grand finale of the Glitch Blocks adventure: warm, clever, and triumphant, with a mystery that has only just begun. Perfect for fans of the Minecraft novels, The Last Kids on Earth, and series that stick the landing. Ages 8-12.
Book 6 of Captain Cubemelon & Friends: The Glitch Blocks.

sections.name: Standalone Novels
sections.blurb: A missing sister in a mountain town. A wealth firm with six months to name a successor. A night photographer who only ever watched. An encrypted ledger going back four centuries. They share nothing but the moment somebody decides not to look away.

desc: Some truths don't stay buried.

Investigative journalist Nora Sutton left Cedar Hollow at eighteen, the summer her sister Lily vanished from the shores of Lake Halcyon. She built a career telling other people's secrets and never once faced her own, and she swore she would never go back to the little mountain town that swallowed the only person who ever truly knew her.
Then the rain stops. A record drought drains the lake to its lowest level in a hundred years, and in the cracked mud of the new lakebed a sunken car returns to the light. There is a body inside.

Nora goes home certain the water has finally given up her sister. It hasn't. The remains belong to Danny Keller, a young man the town spent two decades insisting simply skipped his debts and left, who died the same week Lily disappeared, weighted and chained and sunk. And the deeper Nora digs, the clearer it becomes that everyone in Cedar Hollow agreed, long ago, to forget him.

A drowned boy. A family that owns the water and everyone near it. A father who made a bargain no one should survive. Partnered with an outsider sheriff who distrusts her own department's silence, Nora pulls the one thread that unravels a town. As the drought breaks and the first great storm rolls down into the basin to re-drown the evidence, she learns that the most terrible secret Lake Halcyon ever kept is not the dead it hid.
It is the living.
A propulsive, atmospheric thriller about grief, complicity, and what a community will drown to keep the peace.

Adam Halsey built one of Boston's most trusted wealth firms out of two rooms over a bank and a phone call he made in the worst week of 1987. Forty years later, with four point two billion dollars and fourteen families in his care, he has six months to choose who runs it next, and a diagnosis he has told no one.

He has good hours inside bad days. He has a wife who has been keeping a quiet record since the winter, a daughter who runs the firm's conscience two floors down and never wanted the chair, a head of investments who is already being courted by a rival, and a chief of staff who knows the clients better than the partners do. He has a largest client who tests him weekly, a compliance officer who has begun to ask why he repeats himself, and a small book of old accounts that the next person will be tempted to dismantle, and must not.

THE LAST ADVISER is the story of a succession told in the room where it happens: the annual reviews, the kitchen-table arguments, the late-night work of writing down everything one man knows before he loses the words for it. It is a novel about what a firm is when the firm is a man, what a family is when the money is the wound, and what it costs to hand the truest thing you ever built to someone whose name you are not allowed to say out loud.

desc: From a shoebox apartment five stories above a Manhattan alley, Rory Vance documents the city after dark. A camera, a recorder, a flask, and a creed: do not judge, only witness. He photographs the dreamers and the discarded, the hustlers and the lost, and tells himself the lens keeps him clean. Detachment is his religion. Observation is his alibi.
Then the night begins to look back.

Concrete Mirrors follows a man who has spent years convinced he stands outside the frame. A cryptic mentor presses him to photograph not the decay but the mending. A colder figure draws him into a series of underground social experiments designed to prove that everyone, including the watcher, has a price. As the line between recording a life and steering one dissolves, Rory catches his own reflection in shop windows and no longer recognizes it. The detachment that protected him starts to read like a different kind of hunger.

This is a noir-tinged character study of voyeurism, moral erosion, and the stories we tell ourselves to keep our hands clean. It asks the quiet, dangerous question at the heart of every observer: when you spend your life framing other people, what, exactly, are you building, brick by careful brick?

A literary descent into the ethics of watching. For readers of the urban interiority of Teju Cole's Open City, the psychological unease of Patricia Highsmith, and the city-as-character noir of Paul Auster.

Between 1997 and 2005, an FBI investigation called Operation Bullpen tore the lid off a national racket and produced more than sixty convictions. By the Bureau's own estimate, most of the autographed baseballs, balls signed by Ruth, by Mantle, by Williams, that changed hands in those years were fakes. Stealing First Base is the novel that finally puts a family at the center of that crime.

It begins in 1920, on a train platform in southern Italy, where a nineteen-year-old porter named Russo Massena throws one punch too many and has to run. He runs all the way to America, all the way to Yankee Stadium, carrying nothing but a love of a game he has never seen played. That love becomes an inheritance. It passes down through three more generations of Massenas and Messinas, each one twisting it a little further from the boy on the platform, until it arrives, warped almost beyond recognition, in the hands of his grandson.

Gavin Messina was supposed to hit home runs for the Yankees. Instead he turns out to have the coldest nerve and the most relentless organizing mind in the business. From a warehouse outside Bakersfield he builds the most prolific signature-forgery operation in the country, aging paper in shellac baths and sealed bags of dog food, turning a lifetime of cataloged baseball facts into a machine for manufacturing the past.

But the hand at the center of that machine is not Gavin's. It belongs to Gregory Marino, the quiet prodigy Gavin first handed a pen and a shoebox of signatures across a Long Island kitchen table, when Gregory was eight years old and Gavin told him to try the Mantle. Gregory could already draw anything he saw with complete fidelity. He grows into the finest forger in the country, mixing his own iron gall ink from a chemistry textbook and a set of glass beakers, signing dead legends back to life one ball at a time.

What Gavin does not know is that one of his best customers is a fictitious Japanese trading company, and that every transaction is being recorded by federal agents who have been patient for nine months and are running out of patience fast. He does not know about Steuben Razzburger, the obsessive collector whose lifelong faith in a single baseball card is about to collide with the truth. He does not know that the whole beautiful machine is built, like the game itself, to come apart at exactly the moment of greatest tension.

Moving from a Pullman card game in 1952 to a Las Vegas card show to a federal courtroom in San Diego, Stealing First Base is a sweeping, warmhearted, slyly funny saga about fathers and sons, faith and fakery, and the specific American sadness that arrives when love and ambition meet in the wrong kind of room. The characters are invented. The crimes are not.

For readers of Michael Chabon's The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay, Chad Harbach's The Art of Fielding, and the true-crime spirit of Catch Me If You Can: a multigenerational crime novel about the men who loved baseball clean, and the ones who found a way to love it in the dark.

An encrypted ledger. A four-century-old secret society. A truth ten billion people have been paid not to look at.Elias Thorne is a meticulous financial analyst at Sterling & Price, London’s most prestigious investment firm. He trusts data above all else.

On an otherwise unremarkable Tuesday afternoon, a misfiled encrypted document arrives in his inbox: an ancient ledger of transactions spanning four centuries, encoded in a system that blends modern cryptography with arcane numerological logic. It is, Elias quickly realizes, something that should not exist.

As Elias decodes the outermost layers, patterns emerge that no market model can explain, deliberately orchestrated crashes, engineered bubbles, the systematic redirection of global capital to a hidden network of generational dynasties. The anomaly points toward an entity known only as the Ordo Magnificus Financerum: a centuries-old consortium whose membership spans continents and whose central ambition is permanent control of the world’s economic architecture.

In Paris, Elias meets Isabelle Moreau, a French archivist who has been independently investigating the same anomalies through eighteenth-century financial records. Together they trace the Ordo’s global network: eighty nations, thousands of shell corporations, a coordinated plan called the Chronos Protocol designed to trigger a controlled global financial reset and rebuild the world economy in the Ordo’s permanent image.
The Ordo notices.

From Paris to Geneva to Zurich, Elias and Isabelle are forced underground. A trusted colleague turns out to be an Ordo mole. Sources are systematically targeted. Dr. Aris Thorne, retired economic historian, mentor, the moral conscience of the novel, pays for his involvement with his reputation, then his funding, then everything. He has always known what was coming.

In the Grand Hall of the Ordo’s Geneva headquarters, on the night the Chronos Protocol is to be finalized, Aris Thorne makes the final move. The cost is real. The broadcast that follows reaches every screen on Earth.
The world wakes up.

For readers of Daniel Silva, Robert Harris, and Adam Tooze. The Sterling Conspiracy combines the financial forensics of The Big Short with the institutional conspiracy of John le Carré and the historical sweep of Umberto Eco. A novel that leaves you genuinely unsettled about how the world works.

A globe. A sundial. A maze of mirrors. An echoing grotto. The Athertons have a story their mother once told them, and a chain of clues that has been waiting for them all along.Atherton Manor sits at the end of a long drive, its west wing closed off, its grounds vast and partly overgrown. Eleven-year-old Leo, ten-year-old Clara, and eight-year-old Finn have lived there all their lives. Their mother has been unwell for two years and rarely leaves the second-floor sitting room. Their father carries the household quietly. Mrs. Penberthy, the housekeeper, observes everything and explains almost nothing.

Three years ago, on a rainy afternoon, their mother told them a family story about a stone called the Sunstone, a stone the size of a hen’s egg, hidden by an Atherton ancestor at the top of the highest hill. It does not give brilliance. It reveals the brilliance one already has.
Then they find the first clue.

A globe in the library yields a parchment map. The conservatory sundial reveals a serpent stone. Hidden mechanisms open. A wooden teardrop. A wooden bird. A walk across the south park to the half-mile-distant aviary. A brass cylinder engraved WHERE LIGHT IS NOT WHAT IT SEEMS. A maze of mirrors in the west wing ballroom. A hedge garden labyrinth built over seven summers by a great-aunt who was disinherited from the family. An echoing grotto with an acoustic puzzle. A storm at the folly tower. An observatory at the summit of the eastern hill, with a celestial alignment that requires every artifact they have collected.
And, threading through all of it, a rival group of children with their own reasons for finding the Sunstone first, and a man named Mr. Pemberton who is paying them to do it.

For readers of The Mysterious Benedict Society, The Penderwicks, The Secret Garden, and Frances Hardinge. A quiet, literary middle-grade adventure about three siblings who discover that the path their mother once described, carved through a hundred years of Atherton history, was waiting all along for someone willing to walk it.
Above the manor, the stars come out. The first meeting of the Atherton Discovery Society begins at the end.
Book 1 of The Atherton Manor Mysteries. A portion of every sale is donated to the Kids Future Fund.

books.note: The Atherton Manor Mysteries, Book 2. For young readers, ages 9 to 13
desc: Seven children. Three rooms that answer. An instrument that was never finished.The Athertons found the stones. That was the easy part.

What they have now is a drawing. Twenty journal volumes in an unlit estate room, seventeen of them still on the shelf and three of them gone. A list of nine places on page two hundred and four, six of them carrying a mark and nobody left alive who knows why. And a chamber under the south lawn that was cut to be an ear, tuned to one note, standing empty for as long as the family has been forgetting it was there.

Leo is eleven and has spent his whole life not asking for things. Beatrice keeps the record and will not write down a thing she has not seen. Clara draws. Finn is eight and is not stupid, and there is a difference. Lily is seven and hears what nobody else does. Jasper will not let anybody touch a thing until he knows how thick it is. And Liam, whose father owns the mortgage on half the county, has fourteen days before he is sent home.

Between December and April they go down into the chamber, across the south park to a glass dome that answers only to a song thrush, and a mile and a quarter over wet rock into a grotto that is older than the manor and was a schoolroom before it was anything else. They find four black panels that have been hanging on a ballroom wall being called mirrors for a hundred years. They find a locked drawer, a letter nobody will read to them, and a postscript in the hand of a woman who died in eighteen eighty-one and who asked, in writing, that this family not be the ones to open it.
And in April, for ninety seconds, the thing works.

For readers of The Mysterious Benedict Society, The Penderwicks, and Frances Hardinge. A quiet, literary middle grade adventure about seven children building something out of a drawing, and about what it costs the person who has to answer when you finally learn how to ask.

Best for confident readers of nine and up, and for the adults who end up reading it over their shoulder. The grown-ups in this house are careful, fallible and worth listening to, and they do not take the work out of the children's hands.
Book 2 of The Atherton Manor Mysteries, and a direct sequel. It follows the same seven children from The Starlight Secret Society and opens at their second meeting. Start with Book 1.

books.t: The Tower on the Highest Hill
books.note: The Atherton Manor Mysteries, Book 3. For young readers, ages 10 to 14
desc: Seven children. Ninety-one steps. A building that is on no map.Everybody has been inside the tower. Nobody has ever looked at it.

The story says a man built a tower on the highest hill in his land, and worked there one summer by the light of three candles, and found something. Or made something. Or, depending on which great-aunt tells it, both. The Athertons have been telling that story for two hundred years and not one of them has ever asked when.

Beatrice asks. What she finds is that the man in the story spent forty-one years out on a flat roof in the rain, complaining of it, and never once wrote the word dome. So the building on the hill is not his tower. And there is nothing else on that hill at all.

Between May and midsummer, seven children take a hundred foot cord and a curtain weight up a hill and discover that the outside of a building is bigger than the inside. They open a doorway that somebody bricked up after taking its door off its hinges. They find a bought title filed at the bottom of a box under the coal bills, a man who sold sixty-one men and two furnaces to buy a word he could not say out loud, and four lines in a weather book, written between a note about a flue and a note about a gate, that decided which of four children had failed.
And at the top of ninety-one steps there is a room fourteen feet square, with a stool lying on its side, and a shallow copper dish that nobody alive can explain.

For readers of The Mysterious Benedict Society, Greenglass House, and Frances Hardinge. A quiet, literary middle grade mystery with no villain in it, about who a place belongs to, what a written record does to people who cannot answer it back, and what seven children decide to do when they find out they could make another one.
Best for confident readers of ten and up, and for the adults who end up reading it over their shoulder.
Book 3 of The Atherton Manor Mysteries, and the end of the trilogy. It follows the same seven children from The Starlight Secret Society and The Music of the Spheres. Start with Book 1.

Alex Vance lost everything in 2021. He is about to be offered the chance to lose more.From a one-bedroom apartment in Inwood, looking at a radiator and a Scottish coastline he can no longer afford to remember, Alex Vance is rebuilding a quiet practice. Vance Holdings LLC. A handful of clients. A model that runs on container-data signals and a rule he gives every analyst he hires: find your second trade.
Then Elias Thorne calls.

Thorne, the hedge-fund predator who funded the Hauptmann short that brought Alex back from the dead in 2023, has a new opportunity. A bridge account. A capital-flow scheme that runs through Vance-Orion Continuity Bridge LLC. Forty Wall Street, first Wednesday in April. The numbers work. The pricing is generous. The structure is, if not legal, then within the gray space the SEC has not yet illuminated.
Alex says yes.

Anya Petrova, his analyst, Carnegie Mellon, Berkeley MFE, ex-Halberd Pierce, understands what he has agreed to before he does. So does Liam Chen, his quant. So, eventually, does Reed, his outside counsel of thirty-six years, who lays out the four paths Alex still has and tells him exactly which one he is going to take.
The cost, the bridge account, the firings, the Sterling Dynamics resignation, the morning-after call, the SEC's Vesey Street settlement, is the novel.

For readers of Hernan Diaz Trust, Andrew Sean Greer Less, Paul Murray The Bee Sting. The Fortune Weaver is an austere literary novel about the moral cost of seeing too clearly, written in deliberately spare prose, set inside a finance-thriller chassis.

Eight separately quotable lines that readers across radically different demographics retained: I do not like you. Now eat your soup. Take care of your sister. The boy is here. You are a serious man. Good to see you. The closing reflection: He had not woven anything. He had looked at things until he saw what was actually there. The looking had been the work.
The voice is the value.

The expensive defects are not the ones that get rejected.One of the author's hardcovers is on sale right now with its spine printed upside down. It passed every check. The geometry is exact, every element clears every published limit, and no automated test in existence would catch it, because an inverted spine has perfect measurements.

Every other guide to self-publishing teaches the upload wizard. This one teaches what silently goes wrong: the defects that pass validation, pass review, reach print, and sit on live listings for months while every dashboard reports that everything is fine.
Built entirely from measurement. Drawn from the defect log of a working catalogue of more than seventy titles across KDP and IngramSpark, this manual covers:
Interiors. Mirrored margins, the inside-margin minimum and why you must build above it, page count as a design variable, converter traps and silent clipping.
Paperback covers. Trim against bleed and the margin that scaling quietly eats, the barcode zone, edge safety for type.
Hardcover. Case laminate geometry to five decimal places, the hinge dead zone that paperbacks do not have, rebuilding a spine rather than stretching it, sampling ink from the cover.

IngramSpark. Seven measured caliper records that contradict every published spine calculator, the two failure modes and why only one is fatal, the three separate causes of one identical error message.
Verification. The part that outlasts any particular specification, and the reason to trust the rest.

Twenty figures drawn to scale. Three appendices, including a one-page pre-upload checklist and a complete geometry reference. Every number came off a real file or a live record, and the corrections are left in on purpose, because a rule that was wrong and later fixed teaches more than one that was right all along.

desc: Young Greek-American teenager, from a family steeped in the sponge diving industry of Tarpon Springs, Florida, has his doubts about carrying on the tradition. Even though there is a century of history, including his brother already being a sponge diver, he struggles with even the thought of making dives. Under pressure from his grandmother, his family, and his ancestry, our hero begins to feel like he will never be able to decide, until he meets young, vibrant, WASP, and fully-American tourist. No not tourist... Torn between traditional expectations, modern views, and a decidedly NOT Greek girl, our hero begins to ask himself, “Who Wants to Be Greek?” *** Set before and during the traditional Greek Orthodox celebration of the Feast of the Epiphany, this coming of age tale dives into the traditional lives of the residents of this secluded, idyllic community in Southern Florida and resurfaces with a rich harvest of what it means to be a Greek-American in the computer age. Entwined in the story are descriptions of what it is to be a Tarpon Springs Greek, the religion, the family values, the traditions… and - of course, the dancing!

books.t: Who Wants To Be Greek? Greek Bilingual Edition
desc: The complete novel in English and Modern Greek, side by side, for readers who want the story and the language at once.

At almost eighteen, Giorgos Balaskapoulos lives in Tarpon Springs, Florida, the sponge-diving capital of the world and a loud, loving Greek-American town where everyone seems certain of who they are. Everyone except Giorgos. Torn between his fierce grandmother's traditions, his family's expectations, and a longing he cannot name, he can only answer the question of what he wants with three quiet words: Den gnorizo. I do not know. Then an American girl walks into his uncle's shop, and the careful order of his world begins to shift.

This Bilingual Learning Edition presents the entire coming-of-age story in English paired with Modern Greek, with a phonetic pronunciation guide for every Greek passage and highlighted phrases that teach idiom and feeling, not just vocabulary. Read it as a novel, or grow your Greek a page at a time. It is built for heritage readers reconnecting with the language of their family, for students of Modern Greek who want real narrative instead of drills, and for anyone who has wanted to feel a language from the inside.
Warm, funny, and deeply felt, it is a love letter to the Greek-American experience and to the truth that identity is not a place you arrive at but a dance you learn to make your own.
A companion English Narrative Edition, the complete novel as a single continuous English read, is also available.

sections.name: The Concurrent
sections.blurb: Every world is already in the room. Nobody travels. The only thing that ever changes is the ability to see it, then to touch it, then to speak to it.

books.hook: In 1962 the government moved 660 families to make room for the Moon. It told them when. It never told the others.

sections.name: The American Firsts
sections.blurb: Novels about the first time America did something it now does every week, told from inside the ordinary lives that were standing there when it happened. Each book stands alone, and each carries an Author's Note separating the documented record from invention.

desc: At one minute past noon on the sixteenth of September, 1920, a horse drawn wagon standing outside the Assay Office at the corner of Wall and Broad came apart, and five hundred pounds of cast iron window sash weights went out in every direction at the height of a man.
Thirty three people died. One of them was never named.
The case was never solved. Nobody was ever charged.

One Minute Past Noon follows the hour and the six years after it: a sixteen year old runner who counted his own wages that morning, a lobby porter of fifty eight who was proud of his brass, a Bureau of Investigation agent who came to understand that the case would be lost inside its own paperwork, and the men in Boston and Romagna the Bureau was never quite able to reach.

Every person who dies in this book died in fact, under their own name, with their own age and address and trade, taken from the death certificates of the City of New York and the newspapers of that week. Where the record is silent, the book is silent.
It is a novel about the particular way a country loses something: not in a moment, but slowly, in filing cabinets, by men who are doing their jobs correctly.

The 3200 block of River Road in East Camden is an ordinary working street in the most prosperous decade it will ever have. A shoe repair. A barber with a wooden horse for the children. A corner drugstore, a tailor at the far end, and a path across the back yards that everybody uses and nobody owns.
Two thirds of this novel takes place before anything happens.

That is the point. Every ordinary Tuesday in it is read twice at once: as what it is, and as what you already know it to be. A barber stropping a razor. A shoemaker who has just taken on four years of payments to widen his shop. A boy who has been given a bugle and told to leave it in the closet until his birthday. A woman who cuts through the gate in the fence because everybody cuts through the gate in the fence.

On the morning of Tuesday, the sixth of September, 1949, thirteen people were killed on that pavement in about twelve minutes. Six of them were not from that block. They were passing through, or stopped at the light, or had come in to have a watch looked at.

They are real. They are named here, with their own ages and their own trades, taken from the death certificates, the city directories and the newspapers of that week. Where the record is silent, this book is silent.

And it is not about the man who killed them. He is named three times in sixty eight chapters and is never once given a thought of his own. What the book follows instead is the street, and the sixty years the people on it had to go on living afterward.
The farm was hers before it was his.

It was the old Lawrence Price place, and Lawrence Price was her uncle, and they bought it from his executors in 1919 because it was her family's ground. Six thousand dollars down and six thousand on a mortgage running back to that same estate. Her husband paid the interest twice and then never again.

Nellie Kehoe is fifty-one, short of breath, and has been in and out of hospitals in Lansing for eight months. She notices everything. She notices ten boxes of explosive standing in her barn to blast stumps on a field that has no stumps. She notices two porcelain knobs and a run of wire on the end of a barn on a farm with no electricity. She notices eight shade trees girdled at the same height, and a sound under her floor on a January afternoon, and a crop that was never taken off.

And she concludes almost nothing, because there is almost nothing to conclude, and because the alternative is to say a sentence out loud about her husband that no woman in that township could have said and been believed.

Almost the whole of this novel happens before the eighteenth of May, 1927, in a farmhouse, at a kitchen table. Every ordinary day in it is read twice at once: as what it is, and as what you already know it to be. She gets the day.
Set against it, in short chapters, is the coroner's inquest that followed: three days, fifty-five sworn witnesses, and a proceeding that was never required to find out one thing about her.
Nellie Kehoe left seven words that anybody wrote down. On the list of the dead attached to the jury's finding, between Johns and McFarren, there is an entry that reads Kehoe, Mrs. Andrew.
Hers is the only name on that list that is not a name.
