sections.shelf: For young readers and their grown-ups
sections.blurb: Practical books about earning, building, and handling money, written for readers who are starting early.

desc: On a Saturday afternoon, Maya drew twelve cats with tiny crowns, packaged them as a digital sticker set, priced it at $4, and went to sleep. By Sunday night, eleven strangers had bought it. She made $44 from a device she already owned, using a free app she had downloaded to doodle.
That is what this book teaches.

Side Hustle Jr.: Your Guide to Earning Online is the complete, step-by-step guide for kids ages 10 to 14 who want to start earning money online, not someday, but this week, with tools they can download for free today.

No prior experience required. No startup money. No business license. No expensive software. Just a skill, a device, and the specific steps to turn what you already know how to do into something someone else will pay for.
Seven complete earning paths, one for every type of creator:
• Digital art and sticker packs, sell illustrations, sticker sets, and custom avatars on Etsy and Gumroad
• Websites and blogs, build a site around something you love and grow an audience that pays
• Ebooks, write and sell short guides on topics you already know well
• Print on demand, put your designs on T-shirts, mugs, posters, and phone cases without holding any inventory
• Online courses and video tutorials, teach a skill on video and sell it as a digital product
• Canva and Notion templates, build reusable design and productivity tools others will buy
• Study tools and educational resources, make flashcards, worksheets, and printables teachers and students actually need

Each chapter follows a named kid character through a real challenge, and solves it in a way you can replicate. Every chapter ends with a TRY THIS exercise designed to get you from reading to doing in under an hour.
Also inside:
• The Spend/Save/Reinvest framework for managing your first earnings
• Online safety essentials every kid entrepreneur needs to know
• Time management strategies for building a business alongside school
• How to market your work without a budget or a big following
• What to do when things go wrong, and how to recover fast
• Copyright basics, digital footprint awareness, and reputation protection
• A step-by-step project plan: build, test, improve, and launch
• Platform age requirements, a full glossary, and a guide for parents and educators

This is not a simplified version of adult business advice. Every chapter is honest about the effort required, and specific about exactly what to do next. Readers do not need to finish the book before they start. The structure is built for action.
About the Kids Future Fund

A portion of proceeds from this book supports the Kids Future Fund, a program that provides free entrepreneurship education for young creators who would not otherwise have access to it. Learn more at kidsfuturefund.org.
Side Hustle Jr. is the first book in a series. Forthcoming titles include Side Hustle Jr.: Advanced Earning, Side Hustle Jr.: Managing Your Money, and Side Hustle Jr.: Creator's Playbook.
The oak tree in Chloe's backyard is eighty years old, and it's dying.

A fungal infection, invisible from the outside, has been working through the roots all spring. An arborist has given it a deadline: treatment must happen before the end of August, or the tree is gone. And if the tree goes, the treehouse goes with it, the one with the loose boards and the plank table and the window that never quite latches, the one four kids have been climbing into since they were eight years old.
The treatment costs eight hundred dollars. They have fifty-six.
Alex, Maya, Ben, and Chloe have eleven weeks and one plan: go digital.

Chloe will open an art shop, forest spirits and dragons, digital downloads, sold to strangers on the internet. Ben will build Critter Collector, a creature-catching game he's been designing in his head for months. Alex and Maya will run a tutoring service for students who need help with homework, real help, the kind that teaches you to think, not just the kind that tells you the answer.
None of them have done any of this before.

That means learning to code. Learning digital art software. Learning how platforms work, how payments work, how people find something new when the whole internet is competing for their attention. It means debugging at midnight, questioning whether any of it will work, and sitting in a treehouse one evening asking out loud the question nobody wanted to say: what if we don't make it?

Digital Gold Rush is about what four kids build in one summer, not just the businesses, but the skills, the courage, and the understanding of what it actually means to make something and put it into the world. It's about a game mechanic that finally works after four hours of debugging. About clicking publish and being too scared to look. About a tutoring session where the student finally stops asking for the answer and starts asking for the method.
And it's about an eighty-year-old oak tree that deserves to stand for eighty more.
For readers ages 8 to 12.
Four high school students. One company. One AI that has to work the first time it matters.

Maya writes the code. Liam runs the strategy. Chloe designs the experience. Noah tells the story. They meet at the kickoff for the National Youth Innovation Competition and form The Startup Club, build a company called NovaTech, and name what they are building Catalyst, an AI for the rare pediatric neurological disorders that go undiagnosed for years while children wait.
One of those children is Maya's cousin Rosa. She is twelve. She has been waiting for three.

Building Catalyst is harder than any of them expected: the equity split that almost ends the partnership, the tester who shows them their AI is underdiagnosing patients with darker skin, a data crash, a well-funded rival, and the shortcut that would save the demo and might break everything they came to build.
The Startup Club is a smart, fast coming-of-age novel about ambition, friendship, and the distance between speed and integrity. For readers of The Inheritance Games and Far From the Tree.
A portion of every sale is donated to the Kids Future Fund.
Past midnight, the laptop fan humming, Alex writes the first line of code for a company that does not exist yet. By morning it has a name: Innovate Solutions.

Every startup begins as a flicker, an annoyance most people would grumble about and forget. Alex is not most people. Alex is a problem-solver, and the problem is real: a daily struggle every student knows, and a feeling that technology could fix it. The idea is thrilling and impossibly large at the same time. Building it will take a team, and a team will take trust.

The Digital Founders follows a group of teenage builders as they turn a late-night idea into a real product, and a friendship into a company. They write the code, design the experience, and pitch the dream. They also discover everything the dream does not tell you: the cofounder argument that nearly ends it before it starts, the technical failure with no clean fix, the money decisions that feel impossible at sixteen, the rival who moves faster and plays dirtier, and the ethical crossroads where the fastest path and the right path stop being the same road.

It is a coming-of-age story about ambition and the cost of it, about what you are willing to build and what you are not willing to become to build it. For readers who love stories about creators, competitors, and the messy, exhilarating work of making something out of nothing.
One idea. One team. One shot to prove that the thing they built in a cluttered bedroom can survive contact with the real world.
Seventeen-year-old Al has an ordinary life of calculus quizzes, a part-time job, and a dad lost in the financial pages. Then a single unsolicited invitation arrives, and ordinary ends.

The summons comes from the estate of a billionaire Al has never met, and it is not a condolence card. It is the opening move of a game. To claim a legacy that should not exist, Al must enter the Thorne estate, a house with more rooms than anyone has counted, and solve a chain of puzzles left behind by a man who trusted no one and hid everything.

Inside are a library built like a labyrinth, a vault sealed by an enigma, coded letters that say one thing and mean another, and a blackmail document that proves the family's polished surface is a lie. Every locked door hides a clue. Every clue hides a motive. And somewhere among the relatives, lawyers, and staff who smile too easily, someone is willing to do anything to make sure Al never reaches the end of the game.

The Billionaire's Legacy Game is a twisting inheritance mystery about a teenager pulled into a world of money, secrets, and betrayal, where the real puzzle is not the fortune but who can be trusted to help find it. For readers who love locked-room clues, estate intrigue, and a protagonist who is in far over their head and refuses to fold.
One invitation. One house full of lies. One game with a prize worth killing to keep.
On the morning Alex turns thirteen, the birthday gift is not a gift. It is a single sheet of paper, and it changes everything.

The envelope holds the paperwork for a custodial investment account Alex's parents opened the day Alex was born, quietly growing for thirteen years inside something called an ETF. Alex has never earned a dollar of it, never heard the words compound interest used about real money, and has no idea that one sheet of paper is about to turn into the most important lesson of a lifetime.

What follows is a coming-of-age story told in the language of money. Alex learns how markets rise and fall, why patience pays more than panic, and how a single good habit, repeated for years, becomes a fortune. There is a first real mistake that costs more than allowance. There is a rival whose shortcuts look a lot smarter until they do not. There is an ethical choice that has nothing to do with math and everything to do with character. And there is a market storm that tests whether Alex has learned the one thing the account was meant to teach.

The Growing Fortune is a novel about investing for readers who are old enough to want their own answers and young enough that the answers still feel like an adventure. It teaches the real ideas, diversification, rebalancing, due diligence, the long game, inside a story about growing up, earning trust, and deciding what kind of person you want to be with money and without it.
For young readers, the parents who want to start the conversation, and anyone who wishes someone had explained all of this at thirteen.
Includes a plain-language glossary and a short list of trusted resources for readers who want to keep going.

The most valuable thing you can give a child is not money. It is time.A child born today has one advantage no adult can ever buy back: decades for money to grow. Seeded for Success shows parents, grandparents, and anyone who loves a kid how to turn small, early contributions into a real financial head start by adulthood.
Written in plain language with no jargon and no hype, it walks you through:
Why the first decade decides the trajectory
The real math of compound growth, year by year
How to choose the right account: custodial, 529, taxable brokerage, and Roth options once a child earns income
A giving model where a one-time early gift outlasts ordinary charity
How families, communities, and employers can scale the idea

Not a get-rich scheme and not a lecture: a practical, hopeful guide built on long-term historical averages and one conviction, that every child deserves a fair starting line. For readers of The Opposite of Spoiled and The Index Card.
This book is for general educational purposes only and is not financial, investment, tax, or legal advice. Consult a licensed professional before making financial decisions.
Most online-safety books for kids are built on fear. This one is built on creativity.

Kids today aren't just browsing the internet, they're making things on it. Safe Online Projects for Kids turns that instinct into a strength. Across seven hands-on chapters, children ages 8 to 14 build real projects, code real programs, and create real art, learning to stay safe online as a natural habit rather than a list of scary rules.
By the end of the book, your child will have actually made:
Their own digital workspace and a personal Digital Rules Poster
An original digital drawing and a fully planned illustrated story
An animated character coded from scratch in Scratch
A complete maze game with keyboard controls, scoring, and sound
A real, published webpage they designed themselves
A plan for their own creative project, the Virtual Lemonade Stand

Along the way, safety is woven into every project: strong passwords, privacy settings, smart sharing, kind online behavior, and what to do when something feels wrong. Instead of memorizing warnings, kids learn good digital habits while they're busy building things they're proud of.

Built for grown-ups, too. A complete Facilitator Guide turns every chapter into a ready-to-teach unit, with learning objectives, discussion questions, extension activities, and safety conversation starters. Parents, homeschoolers, librarians, and classroom teachers can run a full digital-literacy unit with no prep. A 25-term glossary makes every concept easy to look up.
Clear enough for an eight-year-old to follow on their own, and never condescending to a fourteen-year-old, this is the digital-skills book that treats kids as the creators they already are.
Perfect for fans of DK's Coding Projects for Kids and Linda Liukas's Hello Ruby, a confident, creativity-first guide to growing up online.
Help your child name, understand, and talk about their feelings, one coloring page at a time.

All About Feelings is a gentle, engaging coloring book for children ages 5 to 8 that introduces young kids to everyday emotions through simple explanations, creative prompts, and fun illustrations to color.

Inside, children will explore feelings such as happy, sad, angry, scared, frustrated, surprised, bored, lonely, jealous, silly, grateful, brave, calm, and kind. Each feeling page gives children a safe way to recognize what they feel, reflect on when they feel it, and express themselves through coloring.
This book is designed to support emotional awareness, early social-emotional learning, and meaningful conversations between children and grown-ups.
Inside this book, you’ll find:
14 feelings to explore
Fill-in reflection prompts on every feeling page
A Feelings Reflection Wheel activity
A special Note to Grown-Ups
Large, kid-friendly coloring pages
Simple language written for ages 5 to 8
Pages designed for crayons, markers, and colored pencils
Perfect for use at home, in classrooms, counseling spaces, homeschool lessons, daycare centers, and quiet-time activities.
All About Feelings helps children learn an important truth early:
All feelings are okay.
All feelings can be talked about.
And every child deserves a safe place to understand what is happening inside.

desc: You do not need a secret. You need a system.Most advice about passive income is built to sell you something. Passive Income Blueprint: Your Action Plan takes the opposite approach: a clear, honest, step-by-step guide for people tired of trading every waking hour for money who want to build something that keeps earning after the work is done.
Written for freelancers, side-hustlers, and small founders, it strips away the hype and walks through the real mechanics of income that does not depend on you showing up every day.
Recognize the income trap that keeps capable people stuck
Build once, earn repeatedly: the foundation of every durable income stream
Choose the right vehicle, from digital products and courses to affiliate sites
Turn a one-time effort into a repeatable, low-maintenance system
Sidestep the five most common pitfalls, including shiny object syndrome
Execute a 30-day ignition plan, one concrete task per day

This book is for general educational purposes only and is not financial, investment, tax, or legal advice. Examples are illustrative and results vary. Consult a qualified professional before making financial decisions.

A second income stream that pays you for owning good businesses, explained without the jargon.Most household budgets ride on a single paycheck. The Passive Income Dividend System lays out a calmer alternative: a layer of regular income paid by established, profitable companies you partly own, built one contribution at a time.
Written for readers new to investing, it turns words like yield, portfolio, and reinvestment into plain, workable steps, with worked dollar examples and honest caveats.
Read a dividend yield correctly and spot the yield trap
Evaluate company health: dividend history, payout sustainability, moats
Understand the four key dividend dates and how a DRIP compounds shares
Build a diversified starter basket using fractional shares
Spread payouts across quarterly cycles for steadier monthly cash flow
Sidestep the five most common beginner pitfalls
Closes with a simple 30-day plan and a 90-day follow-up. This is education, not financial advice; dividends can be cut and figures are illustrative.

Build income that runs when you stop. Not magic. Leverage.This is not another hustle book. It is a plain, operator-focused guide to building income systems that keep working when you step away: the models that actually pay, the first system you can ship now, the implementation that turns one sale into a machine, and the discipline that keeps it running across years of platform change.

For freelancers who have hit the ceiling of billable hours. For employees with a side hustle that never grew up. For solo operators who have been told for years there is a better way and have never seen the actual instructions.
What you getChapter 1 - The Automation Mindset: the shift from trading time for money to building assets that earn without you, and the honest version of what that does and does not mean.
Chapter 2 - Profitable Income Models: six real shapes of automated income that pay in practice, with the trade-offs of each.
Chapter 3 - Your First Automated System: niche, audience, the smallest shippable version, the tool stack, and the first sale.
Chapter 4 - Strategies and Implementation: the systems work that turns a first sale into something that runs, including how to use AI without ruining the work.
Chapter 5 - Scaling and Diversifying: what to do once the system works, when to add a second income source, and what to do with the money once it arrives.
Chapter 6 - Pitfalls and Future-Proofing: why most projects in this category fail, the legal basics, and how to detect trouble before customers do.
Chapter 7 - The 30-Day Plan: a concrete day-by-day sequence to convert one current income loop into a system you can step away from.

Plus three appendices: ready-to-use templates and worksheets, an extended FAQ, and full case studies of operators at every stage (Reena, Mei-Lin, Marcus, Riya, Daniel, and more), each with an honest operating diagnosis.
What this book will not doPromise a specific income figure.
Treat any single platform or tool as a magic bullet.
Pretend "passive" income is ever truly passive. It is leveraged, and leverage still takes work to build.
Pretend automation removes accountability. The book is clear about what stays your job after the system runs.
For the operator who wants the truth about leverage and durability, not the pitch.
A portion of every sale is donated to the Kids Future Fund.
Most AI books promise the world. This one shows you the work.

AI Income Streams is a working operator's guide to building a real business around the AI tools that exist today. It walks through the same sequence the author has used and watched other operators use: pick a specific customer, build a workflow they will pay for, ship it, and expand from there.

The book skips the hype. It does not promise passive income in ninety days. It does not sell a course. What it does instead is lay out a step-by-step path from first customer to scaled business, grounded in concrete case studies and the failure modes that catch most beginners.
Inside, you will find:
The Create-Automate-Monetize framework for building a durable AI-powered offer
Pricing principles that anchor your rates to customer value instead of your time cost
The three constraints that determine whether a niche is worth pursuing: reachability, credibility, and size
The discovery-conversation structure that produces paying clients without a sales script
Platform-specific playbooks for ChatGPT, Claude, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, Notion AI, Perplexity, Runway, GitHub Copilot, and n8n / Make / Zapier
The Ten-Customer Rule for refining your offer through real operator experience
What to do when the platform you depend on changes its terms, its pricing, or its model

What sets this book apart from other AI titles: it covers the legal and professional boundaries that most AI-business books skip. Specific guidance on HIPAA exposure for healthcare workflows. EEOC implications for hiring tools. The licensure line for financial advice. Copyright and IP for AI-generated output. These caveats are named, not glossed.
An Operator Test at the end of every chapter gives you a short written checklist to confirm you can apply what the chapter covered to your own business.
Who this book is for:
Solo operators and freelancers looking to use AI to raise prices or expand without trading more time for money
Small-business owners (one to ten people) ready to integrate AI into delivery, not just experiments
Career-changers looking for a real path to AI-augmented self-employment that is not a course-funnel scheme
Skeptics of AI hype who want a grounded, practical, honest treatment of what these tools actually do

Jeffrey L. Carrier writes for working operators, not aspiring ones. He brings a Department of Defense engineering and communications systems background to a domain that often rewards salesmanship over substance. His framing is the opposite of motivational: pick a customer you can actually meet with this week, pick a tool you can start using today, pick a deliverable you can ship in two weeks. Then ship it.
For readers of The 100 Dollar Startup, Naval Ravikant's Almanack, and Tiago Forte's Building a Second Brain.

When Anthony Cade agrees to deliver a packet of explosive royal memoirs to England, he walks straight into a tangle of stolen jewels, foreign intrigue, and murder at the great house called Chimneys. First published in 1925, this is one of Agatha Christie's most entertaining early thrillers, quick, witty, and full of the misdirection that made her the Queen of Crime.
This Annotated Edition includes the complete novel, an original introduction placing it in Christie's early career, and notes for the modern reader.

desc: The mystery with one of the most famous twists ever written, and the case that made Hercule Poirot a legend.

In the quiet village of King's Abbot, the wealthy Roger Ackroyd is found stabbed in his study. Retired to grow vegetable marrows, Hercule Poirot is drawn back to work by a neighbor's plea, and the solution he uncovers stunned readers in 1926 and has been argued over ever since. The Murder of Roger Ackroyd is widely ranked among the greatest detective novels of all time.

This Annotated Edition includes the complete novel, an original introduction, notes for the modern reader, and a spoiler-walled afterword exploring how Christie pulled off the most debated twist in the genre.

Headnotes for the stories

desc: A forbidden play ruins everyone who reads it to the end. A lost city. A sign you should never have seen.

Robert W. Chambers published The King in Yellow in 1895, and weird fiction has been borrowing from it ever since: the cursed play, the city of Carcosa, the Yellow Sign, the Pallid Mask. Lovecraft's circle borrowed from it, and a prestige TV crime drama sent a new wave of readers hunting for the source. This is that source, complete and unabridged, all ten stories.
What this edition adds to the text:
An original introduction tracing the line from Bierce to Chambers to Lovecraft to today
A headnote before every story, so a first-time reader knows what they are walking into
A Glossary of the Yellow Mythos: Carcosa, Hastur, Hali, the Pallid Mask, the Yellow Sign
Eleven original full-page illustrations in the decadent style of the Yellow Nineties

The four Yellow Sign tales come first, from the future-New York nightmare of "The Repairer of Reputations" to the pure dread of "The Yellow Sign." The rest of the collection follows, including the Paris studio stories that show what Chambers could do with love and loss.

desc: Chambers did not invent Carcosa, Hali, or Hastur. He borrowed all three names from Ambrose Bierce.

In 1886 Bierce wrote a short story about a man lost in a ruined country, trying to find his way back to a city called Carcosa. Five years later he gave a gentle god named Hastur to a shepherd. In 1895 Robert W. Chambers took the names, changed what they meant, and built the most influential nightmare in American weird fiction. This edition prints the pieces in the order they were written, so you can watch a mythology being assembled.
Inside:
Bierce: "An Inhabitant of Carcosa" (1886) and "Haita the Shepherd" (1891)
Chambers: the four Yellow Sign stories from The King in Yellow (1895), plus "The Prophets' Paradise"
An original introduction tracing the line from Bierce to Chambers to Lovecraft and beyond

desc: Two years after The King in Yellow, and Lovecraft never mentioned it.

In 1897 Robert W. Chambers published eight pieces that do not match: three linked tales of a Breton fishing village, two prose poems in which almost nothing happens except death, a violent story about a man who survives his own lynching, a deadpan sea monster hoax certified by scientists who do not exist, and a closing poem.
They do not match because the title is the instruction. Every one of them is a choice, and the consequence arriving late and from the wrong direction.

The reason to own it is the first three. The Purple Emperor is a murder mystery among butterfly collectors and it is genuinely funny. The Messenger takes the same village, the same cast and the same easy comic voice, digs a skull out of a garden with a bullet hole in the forehead, and opens a sixteenth century curse with a family name in it. The reader who has just finished the first story already knows that family. That is the whole design, and it only works in order.
This annotated edition includes:
All eight pieces, complete, in Chambers' own 1897 arrangement
His dedication, his opening poem and his envoi, set as verse
The epigraph he placed at the head of every piece, restored in place
An original introduction, a headnote before all eight, and a glossary of his Brittany
The Messenger, which belongs beside anything in The King in Yellow

An Introduction, plus a headnote for each story
A glossary of Machen's vocabulary
Machen's 1906 introduction and Lovecraft's essay on Machen, reprinted
desc: Before Lovecraft, there was Machen.

In 1894 a Welsh journalist published a short novel about an experiment on a young woman's brain, and about what walked out of her afterwards into London society. The reviewers called it incoherent, nasty and obscene. They were not wrong. They simply could not say what it was obscene about, because Arthur Machen never tells you. He hands you a doctor's notebook, a torn manuscript, a witness who stops mid sentence, and lets you assemble the horror yourself.

Thirty years later H. P. Lovecraft named him the finest living writer of cosmic fear, and borrowed the machinery wholesale. The buried thing that should not be dug up, the remote countryside that keeps older laws, the scholar destroyed by what he pieces together: all of it is in Machen first.
This annotated edition collects the three stories in which his method is complete:
The Great God Pan (1894), the book that made his name and his notoriety
The Inmost Light (1894), its colder London companion, printed with it and overshadowed ever since
The White People (1904), a girl's private diary of things her nurse taught her, and the story many readers call the finest weird tale in English
With original apparatus created for this edition:
An introduction placing Machen at the head of the modern weird tale
A headnote before every story
A glossary of Machen's invented vocabulary, marking plainly which words he never defined
Machen's own 1906 account of how these stories were written and how they were received
H. P. Lovecraft on Arthur Machen, at length, in his own words
Sorcery and sanctity. These are the only realities.

desc: Bierce put it here himself.

In 1886 Ambrose Bierce wrote a very short story about a man lost in a ruined country, trying to find his way back to a city called Carcosa. Nine years later Robert W. Chambers took the name for The King in Yellow, and it has not been quiet since. But the story was not in the first Can Such Things Be? of 1893. Bierce moved it there at the end of his life, together with “Haïta the Shepherd,” the story that names Hastur, when he rearranged his fiction for his Collected Works. That later book is the one Lovecraft read, and it is the one printed here.

These are the twenty-four stories he placed under that title, in his order: “The Death of Halpin Frayser,” “The Damned Thing,” “Moxon’s Master,” “The Moonlit Road,” “An Inhabitant of Carcosa” and the rest.
Inside this edition:
An original introduction on what Chambers took, and the shelf of invented books Bierce built before Lovecraft
A headnote before every story, with dates, settings and what to watch for, and no spoilers
Eighty four notes on the real places, books and battles in the stories, and the invented ones
A glossary that marks every word Bierce invented and never defined, and keeps later additions apart
A comparison of the printings showing what he changed: wife to wives in Carcosa, wolves to bears in Haïta, a daughter to a son in “John Bartine’s Watch”
The Chambers passages that took the names, and a page from The Devil’s Dictionary
The ancient and famous city of Carcosa.

Arthur Machen built The Three Impostors as a trap. Both are anthologised constantly, cut out of the book they belong to. Here they are back inside it, in Machen’s order, doing the work he built them to do.

Gustav Meyrink’s The Golem appeared in 1915 and sold on the order of two hundred thousand copies in its first year. It is not the folk tale. There is no clay servant taking orders. There is a man who cannot be certain whose memories he is having, a ghetto being demolished around him while he works, and a figure that returns to Prague every thirty three years wearing whatever face the city needs it to wear.

The English situation has been peculiar for a century. The only unabridged translation most readers can name is still in copyright. desc: Before Gatsby's parties, there were Dorothy Speare's dancers.

It is 1922. Twenty-year-old Joy Nelson arrives in a New England college town with a country stillness about her and a secret she barely trusts: she can sing. What she finds instead is a set of young people who cannot sit still, the "Excitement-Eaters," who dance until the milk wagons roll, smoke in their dressing gowns, and believe that the instant you stop moving, you lose your grip on life itself.

Swept between the reliable Jim Dalton and the intoxicating pull of the stage, Joy has to answer the question her whole restless generation is dancing to keep from asking: can a girl of the new age hold on to love and the one gift that is truly her own, or must she trade one for the other in the dark?

Published the same season as Fitzgerald's Tales of the Jazz Age, Dancers in the Dark is the flapper novel written from the inside, by a twenty-four-year-old singer who was living its central dilemma herself. Dorothy Speare would go on to Hollywood, where her story of a torn soprano became the classic film One Night of Love (1934); but it all began here, with a tired girl, a pair of silver slippers, and a dedication "To the Girls of Today."

Aboard a steamer bound for Buenos Ayres, the composed American Robert Brent falls into conversation with a shrewd Scotsman named Duncan Fraser. Out of that meeting comes a secret hidden in the Cordilleras of South America, and out of the secret comes a hoard beyond counting: six thousand tons of gold, enough to unsettle every price, wage, debt and treaty in the world.

Brent does not hide his fortune or spend it on palaces. He turns it into a lever. It appeared one year after the Panic of 1893, while America tore itself apart over the gold standard, and it reads today as a sharp fable about abundance promised without cost.

This is a chapbook: a cheap, thin, hand-illustrated popular book of the kind peddlers sold for pennies and children read to pieces. Thousands were printed in the early American republic. Very few survive.

The tale is Charles Perrault's. A nobleman with a repellent blue beard marries a young wife, hands her the keys to his house, forbids her one small room, and leaves. But the names are not Perrault's. Abomelique, Fatima, Irene and Selim came from a hit London stage melodrama of 1798, which is why this nursery book arrives complete with elephants, kettledrums and silken canopies. What a New Haven printer sold to American children was not the fairy tale out of the nursery but the fairy tale as it came back from the theater.

Oliver Herford does not write hatred. He writes contempt, which is a different weapon and a crueler one. His method is to deny these men their scale: an enemy you fear is dangerous, but an enemy who balances his crown on the end of his nose is finished.

Around the war verse sits the rest of a working humorist's year. Epitaphs. Animal poems. Portraits of J. M. Barrie and Mark Twain. And a Devil who opens a Manhattan dress shop to teach fashionable women how to defraud the customs service.

In 1758 a Philadelphia printer gathered twenty five years of his own proverbs into a single speech and gave it to an invented old man to deliver. In the 1870s a Baptist minister began telling a story about a farmer who sold his land to hunt for diamonds, and told it more than six thousand times to put poor students through the university he founded. In 1910 a midwestern writer published a short book claiming that wealth follows a law as reliable as gravity, died the year after, and was forgotten for most of a century until The Secret named him as its inspiration.

They are rarely bound together. They should be. The second is unthinkable without the first, and the third is unthinkable without the second. This edition prints them in reverse order of composition, so that reading it walks the doctrine back to its source.
The Science of Getting Rich (1910), Wallace D. Wattles, complete in all seventeen chapters
Acres of Diamonds, Russell H. Conwell, the lecture itself and not the biography usually bound with it
The Way to Wealth (1758), Benjamin Franklin, the work proper without the Victorian front matter
This annotated edition adds:
An original introduction tracing the lineage from Franklin through Conwell to Wattles, and naming plainly where Conwell's argument turns
A headnote before each of the three works
A glossary of the terms, people and places that have gone dark since
Dost thou love life? Then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of.

desc: Half the universe is running backward, and the half running backward is the half we call alive.

In January 1910 a boy of eleven stood in front of about a hundred Harvard professors and talked for two hours about four dimensional bodies. He had entered the college that autumn as its youngest student. The newspapers took him and did not let go, and he spent most of the thirty years left to him trying to get out from under it. He worked as a clerk. He ran adding machines. He published under invented names.

In 1925, at twenty seven, he published this one under his own. William James Sidis was named for his godfather, and the book is built on an idea of his godfather’s: that a living thing draws on a reserve of energy that physics had already written off.

The argument is simple to state and hard to shake. Almost every law of physics runs the same backward as forward. One does not. Reverse the second law of thermodynamics and heat gathers instead of spreading, and Sidis follows that reversal until it forces him to a Great Collision and then to Great Explosions, a universe beginning in one hot dense event. He raises it in order to discredit the law that led him there. Lemaitre proposed the same shape of beginning, in earnest, six years later.

The figure usually attached to Sidis, an IQ somewhere between 250 and 300, rests on no test that anyone has produced. It is the least interesting thing about him, and this edition sets it aside in a paragraph so the argument can be read on its own terms.
This annotated edition contains:
The complete 1925 text, all nineteen chapters and Sidis’s own preface, set from Harvard College Library’s copy of the first edition, accessioned two months after publication
An original introduction, including a section on what this book is not a prediction of
A headnote before every chapter, marking where he is right, where he is wrong, and where the physics of 1925 simply did not have the tools
A glossary of the private vocabulary he built for the argument
The three figures, from the original cuts
An appendix printing Sidis v. F-R Publishing Corp. entire, the 1940 privacy case that a magazine profile forced on him
Here again there is an appearance of life in objects that we would certainly, in our universe, consider as dead.

desc: Twenty-four stories. Two complete collections. One priest nobody takes seriously.

In 1904 G. K. Chesterton walked across a Yorkshire moor with a small, shabby Catholic curate named John O'Connor, and came off it shaken. The priest looked to the world like a man who knew nothing. He turned out to understand human evil better than the famous journalist did, for the plain reason that people had knelt down in the dark and told him. Seven years later Father Brown walked into print.

He is short and round-faced and shabby. He carries a brown paper parcel and an umbrella he keeps losing. He blinks a great deal. Everybody in every story underrates him, which is exactly how he works, because Brown does not reason outward from cigar ash and the knees of trousers. He goes inside the murderer, thinks the man's thoughts, wants what the man wanted, and then he knows.

This edition prints The Innocence of Father Brown (1911) and The Wisdom of Father Brown (1914) complete and in order, the way Chesterton's first readers met them, so the arc of Flambeau runs unbroken from the most wanted criminal in Europe to the priest's closest friend. The Blue Cross, The Queer Feet, The Invisible Man, The Hammer of God, The Sign of the Broken Sword, The Man in the Passage, and eighteen more.
What makes this edition different
A new introduction on the real priest behind Father Brown, and on the method he handed over
A headnote in front of each of the twenty-four stories
A glossary of the period terms and references the plots actually run on
A Chesterton timeline and a ten-question reader's guide
A straight, factual note on the television series: which eight episodes carry the title of a story printed here, and how far they wander from it
The whole text, unabridged and unmodernised, with Chesterton's own punctuation left alone

These stories are over a century old and this edition does not pretend otherwise. Where one carries racial or national material a reader today should see rather than absorb, the headnote says so before you start. Nothing has been cut.
Fair warning if the television brought you here. The original is sharper, stranger and a good deal darker. That is the reason to read it.

paragraphs: Marina counted nine mourners who still spoke Alexandrian Greek and seventeen who did not. The funeral was small. Her grandmother had wanted it small, and the people who came spoke either the Alexandrian Eudoxia had carried for sixty-five years in Athens or the Athenian her daughter had refused to inherit and refused to replace. Anastasia received condolences without correcting anyone's Greek. Marina, who had spent the morning cataloguing the mourners by their accents because it was the only thing she could think to do, stood a half step behind her mother and held her gloves.

The cemetery was on the south slope of the city. The Greek-Egyptian section was a small plot at the back, where the cypresses thinned and the city spread out toward Piraeus in the afternoon light. Eudoxia had picked the plot twenty years ago, paid for it in francs converted on a holiday, and told no one until the paperwork had to be witnessed. That was Eudoxia. Marina had organized the witnesses herself. She had been twenty-four, a graduate student, and her grandmother had said this is the kind of thing I prefer to do while I can still sign my own name.

The priest read in Greek with a slight Cypriot inflection. Eudoxia had liked him because he did not pretend to be Alexandrian. The reading was short. Eudoxia had wanted the prayers and not the speeches, and the family had honored it. No one stood to say anything about who she was. Marina had been grateful for it during the service and was grateful for it again now, watching the small line of mourners form to embrace her mother. She would not have known what to say. She had spent a career writing about the women her grandmother had been one of, and had not known how to be in a room of them as a granddaughter.

Anastasia stood very straight. The last of the early-autumn warmth still hung in the cypresses. A drop of sweat moved down the back of Anastasia's neck and Marina watched it without reaching to wipe it. Her mother would not have wanted her to. The line moved forward.

The woman who took Anastasia's hand was perhaps eighty. She wore a small dark hat with a veil and a thin gold cross. She did not introduce herself. Anastasia thanked her in formal Greek. The woman moved past Anastasia toward Marina and stopped in front of her and looked at her for long enough that Marina noticed Anastasia notice. The woman's hands were dry and careful when she took Marina's. She held them.
"I knew your grandmother in Alexandria," the woman said. "I am Lysandra Kallistos."
Lysandra did not release her hands. "There are some things she did not finish," she said. "Pragmata pou meinan anoichta. You will know what to do."

The Alexandrian Greek was perfect. The phrase was Eudoxia's phrase. Marina had heard her grandmother use it about a half-translated letter, about a sweater she had not finished, about a question Marina had asked her once at seventeen and that Eudoxia had refused to answer that day and had not returned to. Things left open. Marina did not move her hands.
"I do not know what you mean," she said.
